title: Nestor's indecision: the brooding sea
greek: ὡς ὅτε πορφύρῃ πέλαγος μέγα κύματι κωφῷ (hōs hote porphurēi pelagos mega kumati kōphōi)
short: Nestor hesitates like a great sea heaving with a silent swell, which waits for a decisive wind from Zeus before it rolls either way.
body: Nestor sees the wall breached and cannot decide whether to join the fighting or find Agamemnon. The sea in the simile 'heaves' (πορφύρῃ) with a 'dumb' wave (κύματι κωφῷ). LSJ explains this as a swell whose waves do not break, and Leaf as a ground-swell raised by a distant storm. The sea foresees the paths of the winds but does not roll forward to either side 'until some settled gale cometh down from Zeus'. Monro notes that πορφύρω is related to πορφύρεος, which first meant any dark, troubled colour. Murray's 'heaveth darkly' keeps both senses. The verb is used of a troubled heart in the Odyssey (4.427). The simile turns deliberation into a natural force: a mind divided two ways, waiting for an outside push. At last 'this seemed to him the better', the usual formula for a decision.

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 14.16
D. B. Monro, Homer: Iliad, Books XIII-XXIV, with notes (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1897), note on 14.16-19
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed.), s.v. πορφύρω

title: The Greek camp: ships beached in rows
greek: τῶ ῥα προκρόσσας ἔρυσαν (tō rha prokrossas erusan)
short: The beach was too narrow, so the ships were beached in rows filling the bay; the wounded kings' ships lay farthest from the fighting.
body: The wounded kings, Diomedes, Odysseus and Agamemnon, come up from ships that lie far from the battle. The shore, though broad, could not hold the whole fleet, so the Greeks drew the ships up 'in rows' (προκρόσσας, Leaf: 'in rows or ranks, one behind another'). They filled 'the wide mouth of all the shore that the headlands shut in'. Leaf sets out two interpretations of lines 31-2, depending on which ships counted as 'first'. Monro explains that the wall was built along the line of ships furthest from the sea, which is why the kings' ships, nearest the water, were out of the fighting. This geography matters for Books 12-16, as the fighting moves from the wall to the sterns of the ships, especially the ship of Protesilaus (13.681; 15.704-25).

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 14.30-35
D. B. Monro, Homer: Iliad, Books XIII-XXIV, with notes (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1897), note on 14.31

anchor: not shame to flee from ruin
title: Agamemnon proposes flight for the third time
greek: οὐ γάρ τις νέμεσις φυγέειν κακόν, οὐδ' ἀνὰ νύκτα (ou gar tis nemesis phugeein kakon, oud' ana nukta)
short: Despairing, Agamemnon proposes launching the ships at night; Odysseus rebukes him sharply and Agamemnon backs down.
body: Agamemnon fears Zeus wants the Achaeans to perish 'nameless, far from Argos'. He proposes launching the front row of ships and fleeing by night: 'there is no nemesis in escaping ruin' (LSJ cites this line for νέμεσις). This is his third such proposal. In Book 2 he made it as a test (2.110-41), in Book 9 in earnest (9.17-28). Odysseus answers with unusual violence: 'what a word has escaped the barrier of your teeth!' He wishes Agamemnon commanded some 'inglorious army', and warns that once the ships are launched the men will stop fighting and look only for escape. Agamemnon gives way and asks for better counsel, which Diomedes supplies. Leaf observes that the proposal has 'already been twice made, in B and I', and suggests the whole scene may come from a different continuation of Book 12.

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (2nd ed., 1902), Introduction to Book XIV, pp. 63
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed.), s.v. νέμεσις

anchor: wind the skein of grievous wars
title: 'Winding off the skein of war'
greek: τολυπεύειν ἀργαλέους πολέμους (tolupeuein argaleous polemous)
short: Odysseus uses a wool-working word: Zeus has given the Greeks war to 'wind off like yarn' from youth to old age, until they die.
body: τολύπη is the ball of wool wound up after carding, and τολυπεύω means to wind it off for spinning (LSJ). Used figuratively, it means to carry a task through to the end. Leaf glosses it 'to wind up', and LSJ here 'endure'. Odysseus says Zeus has granted the Greeks to 'wind off grievous wars from youth to old age, until we perish every one'. Women's household work becomes an image for a man's lifelong labour of war. The Odyssey uses the same verb for finishing a war (Od. 1.238). It also gives Penelope a pun on it, 'I wind off wiles' (Od. 19.137), she whose trick was weaving and unweaving a web. Homer often uses textile words for plotting and fate: compare Helen weaving the war into her tapestry (3.125-8).

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed.), s.v. τολυπεύω
W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 14.86

anchor: in Thebe the heaped-up earth covereth
title: Diomedes' lineage: Tydeus and the house of Oeneus
greek: Τυδέος, ὃν Θήβῃσι χυτὴ κατὰ γαῖα καλύπτει (Tudeos, hon Thēbēisi chutē kata gaia kaluptei)
short: The youngest of the kings justifies speaking by his descent: grandson of Oeneus of Calydon, son of Tydeus, who died and was buried at Thebes.
body: Diomedes apologises for his youth (compare Nestor's remark at 9.57-8) and claims a right to speak from his lineage. Portheus' sons were Agrius, Melas and Oeneus. Tydeus, son of Oeneus, 'went wandering' to Argos, married a daughter of Adrastus, and died in the expedition of the Seven against Thebes, where he lies buried. Leaf notes that Pausanias saw a tomb of Tydeus at Thebes (9.18.2), though another legend placed his grave at Eleusis. The Iliad does not say why Tydeus left home. Later mythographers report that he fled after a homicide (Apollodorus 1.8.5). Leaf thinks the genealogy 'untimely' and unlike Diomedes' usual plain speech, perhaps an addition by the genealogical school of poets. Line 114 was athetized by Zenodotus. Diomedes is always measured against his father: compare Agamemnon's taunt at 4.370-400.

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 14.114
W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (2nd ed., 1902), Introduction to Book XIV, pp. 63
Pausanias 9.18.2 (tomb of Tydeus at Thebes)

anchor: nine thousand warriors, or ten thousand
title: Poseidon's shout
greek: ὅσσον τ' ἐννεάχιλοι ἐπίαχον ἢ δεκάχιλοι (hosson t' enneachiloi epiachon ē dekachiloi)
short: Disguised as an old man, Poseidon cheers Agamemnon, then shouts as loud as nine or ten thousand men: lines reused from Ares' scream in Book 5.
body: Poseidon comes 'in the likeness of an old man', takes Agamemnon's right hand and predicts a Trojan rout. Then he shouts across the plain as loud as nine or ten thousand warriors. The couplet repeats the scream of the wounded Ares (5.859-61), and lines 151-2 repeat 11.11-12. Leaf finds it comic that a god trying to escape Zeus's notice in human form should give a superhuman shout. It reminds him of 'a favourite joke of modern burlesques'. He also notes that the vague 'old man' breaks Homer's usual rule that a god takes the form of a named person, as Poseidon did with Calchas and Thoas in Book 13. Other readers see the repetition as normal in formulaic composition, where a ready-made line takes new force from its context.

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2 (2nd ed., 1902), Introduction to Book XIV, pp. 63

title: The Deception of Zeus (Dios Apatē)
greek: ὅππως ἐξαπάφοιτο Διὸς νόον αἰγιόχοιο (hoppōs exapaphoito Dios noon aigiochoio); Διὸς ἀπάτη
short: Hera seduces Zeus on Mount Ida and has Sleep overcome him, so that Poseidon can help the Greeks: the Iliad's great comic interlude among the gods.
body: Hera sees Poseidon at work and Zeus on Ida, and plans to beguile him. She adorns herself, borrows Aphrodite's love-charm, bribes Sleep, and lies with Zeus on Gargarus. Ancient readers called the episode Διὸς ἀπάτη, 'the Deception of Zeus'. Leaf calls it 'radiant with humour, grace, and healthful sensuousness', the work of a single hand. Plato objected that it showed the king of the gods forgetting all his plans out of desire (Republic 390b-c). Modern critics have debated its unusual language: Dihle took it as a sign of late composition, while Janko defends its artistry. Its cosmogony has been compared to Near Eastern myth (Burkert), a link Kelly disputes. The episode reverses Book 2, where Zeus deceived Agamemnon with a dream: now the deceiver is deceived. Zeus wakes in fury at the start of Book 15.

anchor: With ambrosia first did she cleanse
title: Hera's toilette: an arming scene for love
greek: ἀμβροσίῃ μὲν πρῶτον ἀπὸ χροὸς ἱμερόεντος λύματα πάντα κάθηρεν (ambrosiēi men prōton apo chroos himeroentos lumata panta kathēren)
short: Hera bathes, anoints, dresses and adorns herself item by item, like a warrior arming, in a type-scene shared with Aphrodite in the Hymn and the Odyssey.
body: Hera goes to a chamber that Hephaestus built with a secret bolt. She cleanses herself with ambrosia and anoints herself with an oil whose scent would reach earth and heaven. She plaits her hair and puts on a robe that Athena wove, golden brooches, a girdle with a hundred tassels, earrings, a veil 'white as the sun' and sandals. The sequence works like an arming scene (Agamemnon 11.15-46, Akhilleus 19.364-91), building item by item towards an attack. Here the weapon is beauty. The closest parallels are Aphrodite's preparations in the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite: a fragrant shrine at Paphos, shining doors shut, the Graces bathing and anointing her (58-67). Compare also Od. 8.362-6. Leaf discusses the 'perfumed' oil (172). Monro explains the κρήδεμνον as a mantle covering head and shoulders but leaving the face free.

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 14.170-172

title: Hera's earrings: trigléna moróenta
greek: ἕρματα ... τρίγληνα μορόεντα (hermata ... triglēna moroenta)
short: Two obscure epithets for earrings, already disputed in antiquity; Murray follows the view that they had three clustered, berry-like drops.
body: The line recurs only at Od. 18.297-8, among the suitors' gifts to Penelope, and Leaf notes that earrings are mentioned nowhere else in Homer. τρίγληνος is probably formed from γλήνη, 'eyeball, bead'. Ancient critics explained it variously as 'with three beads', 'three-eyed' or 'made of three figures' (LSJ). μορόεις is still more obscure. Proposed meanings include 'sparkling'; 'wrought with labour' (Hesychius); 'immortal' (Apollonius' Lexicon); and 'like mulberries', from μόρον (Ernesti), which Monro adopts as 'clustering'. Murray's 'three clustering drops' follows that view. Leaf points to Helbig's comparison with archaic pendant earrings with three drops. Formulas like this kept words whose meaning had already been lost to the Greeks themselves.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed.), s.v. τρίγληνος
Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed.), s.v. μορόεις

title: Oceanus and Tethys, origin of the gods
greek: Ὠκεανόν τε θεῶν γένεσιν καὶ μητέρα Τηθύν (Ōkeanon te theōn genesin kai mētera Tēthun)
short: Hera's cover story names Oceanus as the origin of the gods and Tethys as mother: a cosmogony unlike Hesiod's, and much debated.
body: Hera says she is going to visit Oceanus, 'origin of the gods', and 'mother Tethys', who raised her when Zeus thrust Cronos beneath the earth. She will end their long quarrel, for they have kept apart from the marriage bed. Sleep later calls Oceanus the source 'from whom they all are sprung' (14.246). Leaf notes that Tethys appears only here in Homer, and that nowhere else is Oceanus called the ancestor of the gods. In Hesiod both are Titans, children of Earth and Heaven (Theogony 133-6), and parents of the rivers and Oceanids. Plato quotes the line as an early statement that everything comes from flux and motion (Theaetetus 152e). Walter Burkert compared Apsu and Tiamat, the estranged primeval waters of the Babylonian Enuma Elish. Adrian Kelly has challenged the parallel. The quarrel story itself is Hera's invention.

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 14.201
Hesiod, Theogony 133-136
Plato, Theaetetus 152e

title: Aphrodite's embroidered band (kestos himas)
greek: κεστὸν ἱμάντα ποικίλον (keston himanta poikilon)
short: Aphrodite lends Hera the band that holds love, desire, intimate talk and persuasion; later called the cestus, the girdle of Venus.
body: From her breast Aphrodite loosens 'the embroidered strap', which holds 'all manner of allurements': love (φιλότης), desire (ἵμερος), intimate talk (ὀαριστύς), and the persuasion that steals the wits even of the wise. κεστός means 'stitched, embroidered', from κεντέω, 'to pierce' (LSJ). Only later did it become a noun, 'the cestus'. Monro, following Helbig, thinks it was not a garment but 'simply a charm', carried in the bosom for safety. Leaf compares the veil that Leucothea gives Odysseus as a magic charm (Od. 5.346). Christopher Faraone discusses the kestos among Greek erotic amulets. The irony is that Aphrodite, champion of the Trojans, unknowingly helps the Greeks. Hera 'smiled, and smiling laid it in her bosom'. Murray's 'zone' (girdle) keeps the traditional English picture.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed.), s.v. κεστός
D. B. Monro, Homer: Iliad, Books XIII-XXIV, with notes (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1897), note on 14.214-217
W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 14.214-219

title: Hypnos, brother of Thanatos
greek: Ὕπνος, κασίγνητος Θανάτοιο (Hupnos, kasignētos Thanatoio)
short: Sleep and Death are brothers, children of Night; here Sleep is a comic, timid, bribable god, but in Book 16 the brothers carry Sarpedon home.
body: Hesiod makes Sleep and Death children of Night (Theogony 211-12). They live together in the underworld, Sleep gentle to men and Death with a heart of iron (Theogony 756-66). Leaf calls their brotherhood 'a familiar allegory in all literature'. In the Iliad the pair carry the dead Sarpedon home to Lycia (16.671-83). The scene was painted on the Euphronios krater (c. 515 BC), where winged Sleep and Death lift Sarpedon's body. Homer's language often treats death as sleep: Iphidamas 'slept a sleep of bronze' (11.241), and Promachus 'sleeps' at 14.482-3. Virgil places Sleep, 'kinsman of Death', at the entrance to the underworld (Aen. 6.278). In Book 14, though, Sleep is a lively, comic personality: wary of Zeus's anger, he refuses one bribe and accepts another out of love for Pasithea.

sources.cite: Hesiod, Theogony 211-212, 756-766

anchor: Lemnos, the city of godlike Thoas
title: Lemnos, city of Thoas
greek: Λῆμνον ... πόλιν θείοιο Θόαντος (Lēmnon ... polin theioio Thoantos)
short: Hera flies by real landmarks of the northern Aegean to Lemnos, where she finds Sleep; why Sleep is there no one knows.
body: Hera's route follows real geography: from Olympus over Pieria and Emathia, along the snowy Thracian mountains, down to Athos, and across the sea to Lemnos. Thoas, king of Lemnos, is mentioned again at 23.745 and is not the Aetolian leader of the same name. In later legend he is the father of Hypsipyle, who saved him when the Lemnian women killed their men (Apollonius, Argonautica 1.620-6). Leaf admits that we cannot guess why Sleep is found on Lemnos, since no cult of Hypnos there is known. He quotes a scholiast's ingenious explanation. Lemnos was Hephaestus' island, where he fell from heaven (1.590-4), and Hephaestus married a Grace (18.382-3), so Sleep had come courting her sister. That links neatly with Pasithea later in the scene.

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 14.230
Apollonius of Rhodes, Argonautica 1.620-626

title: Hera, Heracles and the storm to Cos
greek: ὑπέρθυμος Διὸς υἱός (huperthumos Dios huios)
short: Sleep recalls helping Hera before: she drove Heracles off course to Cos while Zeus slept, and Zeus woke in fury.
body: When Heracles sailed home after sacking Troy, Sleep lulled Zeus while Hera raised storms and drove Heracles to Cos. This was the first sack of Troy, in the reign of Laomedon (5.638-42). Zeus woke, hurled the gods about his palace, and would have thrown Sleep into the sea if Night had not protected him. Leaf notes that Heracles is not named until line 266, and that the Iliad returns to the story when Zeus reminds Hera how he punished her by hanging her from heaven with anvils on her feet (15.18-30). Apollodorus tells the same story of the storm, the landing on Cos and Hera's punishment (Library 2.7.1). Hera's hatred of Heracles runs from his birth (19.96-133). Sleep's story warns that deceiving Zeus has consequences, and Book 15 proves it.

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 14.250
Apollodorus, Library 2.7.1

title: Night, subduer of gods and men
greek: Νὺξ δμήτειρα θεῶν ... καὶ ἀνδρῶν (Nux dmēteira theōn ... kai andrōn)
short: Zeus held back his anger out of awe for Night: the only power before which the Iliad's Zeus shows fear.
body: Sleep fled to Night, 'subduer of gods and men', and Zeus held back, angry as he was, because 'he had awe lest he do aught displeasing to swift Night'. No other passage shows Zeus deferring to a deity in this way. Leaf rejects Zenodotus' reading μήτειρα ('mother') for δμήτειρα, 'subduer' (Autenrieth), and compares Sleep 'the all-subduer' (24.5). Night belongs to the oldest layer of the gods. In Hesiod she comes from Chaos together with Erebus (Theogony 123-5) and bears Sleep and Death (211-12), and her dread house stands at the edge of the world (744-57). Later Orphic cosmogonies made Night the first principle, and Aristotle refers to 'theologians who generate the world from Night' (Metaphysics 1071b27). The line hints that even Zeus's order rests on older powers.

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 14.259
G. Autenrieth, A Homeric Dictionary (trans. R. Keep, 1876), s.v. δμήτειρα
Aristotle, Metaphysics 12.6, 1071b27

title: Pasithea and the Graces (Charites)
greek: Χαρίτων μίαν ὁπλοτεράων ... Πασιθέην (Charitōn mian oploteraōn ... Pasitheēn)
short: Sleep refuses Hera's golden throne but accepts the promise of Pasithea, one of the Graces, whom he has always loved.
body: Sleep turns down a golden throne made by Hephaestus, but Hera wins him by promising one of the 'youthful Graces', Pasithea, as his wife. The Charites personify charm and beauty. They made Aphrodite's robe (5.338) and bathe her at Paphos (Od. 8.364), and a Charis is the wife of Hephaestus (18.382-3). Leaf notes that in Homer their number is indefinite and ὁπλότεραι means 'youthful' rather than 'younger'. Hesiod fixes them at three, Aglaea, Euphrosyne and Thalia, daughters of Zeus and Eurynome (Theogony 907-11), and gives Aglaea to Hephaestus (945-6). Pausanias discusses the varying numbers and names of the Graces in different cults (9.35). The scene is gently comic: the god who masters everyone is himself a lovesick suitor, who makes Hera swear her promise.

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 14.267
Hesiod, Theogony 907-911, 945-946
Pausanias 9.35

title: The great oath of the gods: Styx and the Titans
greek: ἀάατον Στυγὸς ὕδωρ (aaaton Stugos hudōr)
short: Sleep makes Hera swear by the water of Styx, touching earth and sea and calling the Titans below as witnesses.
body: The oath by Styx was the most binding oath a god could swear. In Hesiod a god who swears falsely by its water lies breathless for a year and is shut out from the gods' councils for nine more (Theogony 775-806). Hera must hold the earth with one hand and the sea with the other, so that the gods below with Cronos may be witnesses, and she names the Titans in Tartarus. Leaf calls the epithet ἀάατος an unsolved problem, while Monro suggests 'not to be trifled with', i.e. inviolable. Monro explains the touching of earth and sea as calling the powers beneath both, comparing Althaea beating the earth to summon Hades (9.568-9). Leaf notes that only the older dynasty of gods could serve as witnesses to an Olympian, since the Olympians do not swear by one another. Hera swears by Styx again at 15.36-46.

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 14.271, 14.279
D. B. Monro, Homer: Iliad, Books XIII-XXIV, with notes (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1897), note on 14.271-273
Hesiod, Theogony 775-806

title: The language of gods and men: chalcis and cymindis
greek: χαλκίδα κικλήσκουσι θεοί, ἄνδρες δὲ κύμινδιν (chalkida kiklēskousi theoi, andres de kumindin)
short: Sleep hides in a fir tree as a mountain bird with two names, one used by gods and one by men: one of Homer's few 'divine words'.
body: Sleep perches unseen in the tallest fir on Ida, in the form of a clear-voiced mountain bird. Homer gives it two names, as he does for a few other things: Briareus/Aegaeon (1.403-4), Batieia/the tomb of Myrine (2.813-14), and Xanthus/Scamander (20.74). Monro remarks that the divine name is the one with a good meaning, χαλκίς, 'bronze-coloured'. Calvert Watkins linked these pairs to an Indo-European tradition of a 'language of gods' set against a 'language of men'. The bird cannot be identified. Aristotle says the kymindis is rarely seen and lives in the mountains (History of Animals 615b6, cited by LSJ), and Leaf thinks it was probably nocturnal, an owl or a night-hawk. Leaf also cites D'Arcy Thompson's suggestion that the name hints at the 'bronze sleep' of death.

sources.cite: W. Leaf, The Iliad, vol. 2, Books XIII-XXIV (2nd ed., London: Macmillan, 1902), note on 14.291

anchor: god of the two strong arms
title: Hephaestus amphigyēeis: strong-armed or lame?
greek: ἀμφιγυήεις (amphiguēeis)
short: Hephaestus' epithet may mean 'strong in both arms' (Murray's rendering) or 'crooked in both feet', lame; both traits belong to the smith-god.
body: Murray follows the ancient interpretation 'strong in both arms', or ambidextrous (Autenrieth), deriving the word from γυῖον, 'limb'. LSJ prefers 'with both feet crooked, lame'. Hesiod uses the word as a name, which Evelyn-White translates 'the famous Lame One' (Theogony 945). Hephaestus' lameness is plain elsewhere: he limps (18.411, 417), and he tells how Zeus hurled him from heaven to Lemnos (1.590-4). In the Odyssey he complains of being born lame (Od. 8.308-11). Thin legs and a powerful chest and arms (18.410-15) both fit a craftsman-god, so the dispute cannot be settled from context. In this book he is the maker of divine objects: Hera's bolted chamber (14.166-8), and the golden throne and footstool she offers Sleep as a bribe.

sources.cite: Liddell-Scott-Jones, A Greek-English Lexicon (9th ed.), s.v. ἀμφιγυήεις
G. Autenrieth, A Homeric Dictionary (trans. R. Keep, 1876), s.v. ἀμφιγυήεις
Hesiod, Theogony 945

title: Zeus's catalogue of loves
greek: Ἰξιονίης ἀλόχοιο (Ixioniēs alochoio)
short: Overcome by desire, Zeus tells Hera he never wanted anyone so much, and tactlessly lists his previous loves; Aristarchus rejected the lines.
body: Zeus swears he has never desired anyone as he desires Hera now. He then names his earlier loves and their children: the wife of Ixion (Dia, Monro), mother of Peirithous; Danaë, mother of Perseus; 'the daughter of Phoenix' (Europa), mother of Minos and Rhadamanthys; Semele, mother of Dionysus; Alcmene, mother of Heracles; Demeter, Leto, and Hera herself. (Murray's printed 'Acmsius' is a misprint for Acrisius, Danaë's father.) Aristophanes and Aristarchus athetized lines 317-27 as untimely, since listing rivals would sooner alienate Hera than win her (Leaf). Leaf nicknames it the 'Leporello-catalogue', after Don Giovanni's servant, and finds its style Hesiodic, like the Catalogue of Women. The comedy may be the point. Milton reworks the scene after the Fall: Adam tells Eve that her beauty never so inflamed his sense (PL 9.1029-33), then leads her to a bed of flowers.

title: The sacred marriage on Gargarus
greek: τοῖσι δ' ὑπὸ χθὼν δῖα φύεν νεοθηλέα ποίην (toisi d' hupo chthōn dia phuen neothēlea poiēn)
short: Wrapped in a golden cloud, Zeus and Hera lie together while the earth sends up lotus, crocus and hyacinth: Homer's most 'romantic' scene.
body: Zeus wraps them in a golden cloud that not even the Sun can see through. Beneath them the earth sends up fresh grass, dewy lotus, crocus and hyacinth, and shining dew drips from the cloud. Leaf calls it 'the most romantic' passage in Homer, comparable in its sympathy of nature with Poseidon's journey (13.27-9). He speaks of the union as a ἱερὸς γάμος, the sacred marriage of the sky-god with a goddess, at which the earth bursts into growth. Virgil turned it into allegory: the Father, Aether, descends in fertile rain into the lap of his joyful wife (Georgics 2.325-7). Milton echoes it three times. Adam smiles on Eve 'as Jupiter On Juno smiles' (PL 4.499-501). Eden's bower has 'violet, Crocus, and hyacinth' underfoot (4.700-2). After the Fall, 'flowers were the couch' (9.1039-41). Then Zeus sleeps, 'overmastered by sleep and love', and Hera's plan is complete.

title: Poseidon leads: the exchange of armour
greek: ἀρήϊα τεύχε' ἄμειβον (arēïa teuche' ameibon)
short: With Zeus asleep, Poseidon openly leads the Greeks, has the best men take the best armour, and brandishes a terrible sword like lightning.
body: Now that Zeus sleeps, Poseidon openly urges the Argives on. The best fighters are to take the largest shields and helmets and the longest spears, and pass their smaller arms to weaker men. The wounded kings organise the exchange, and Poseidon leads with a long sword 'like unto the lightning', which it is 'not permitted' (οὐ θέμις) for anyone to meet in battle. Critics have found the scene awkward. Leaf calls a general change of armour in the thick of battle 'partly unintelligible, partly ludicrous'. He notes that Aristarchus athetized 376-7, and that the grand divine sword does nothing afterwards. Monro agrees that exception has been taken 'not without reason'. Within the story, the open leadership contrasts with Poseidon's secret help in Book 13 (13.351-7): the difference is that Zeus is now asleep.

title: Strife stretched tight: Poseidon against Hector
greek: αἰνοτάτην ἔριδα πτολέμοιο τάνυσσαν (ainotatēn erida ptolemoio tanussan)
short: Poseidon and Hector 'strain' the strife of war; the sea surges to the ships, and the armies' cry outdoes sea, fire and wind.
body: 'Then verily were strained the cords of war's most dreadful strife' by Poseidon and Hector. The image of war as a rope pulled tight goes back to 13.358-60. Leaf objects that treating a god and a mortal as equal powers is un-Homeric. Monro takes the surge of the sea up to the huts as the sea rising in sympathy with its god. The battle-cry is then measured by three negative comparisons. Not the wave driven ashore by the North Wind, not a forest fire in a mountain glen, not the wind roaring in tall oaks is as loud as the shout of Trojans and Achaeans. This 'not so... as' form, which piles up natural forces only to say that the human din exceeds them all, is unusual in Homer.

title: Aias' two baldrics (telamōnes)
greek: ᾗ ῥα δύω τελαμῶνε περὶ στήθεσσι τετάσθην (hēi rha duō telamōne peri stēthessi tetasthēn)
short: Hector's spear strikes where Aias' two straps cross on his chest, one for the shield and one for the sword, and they save him.
body: Hector's spear hits Aias where the two baldrics are stretched across his chest, the strap of his shield and the strap of his silver-studded sword, and they protect his flesh. Leaf and Monro disagree over details. Leaf places the sword-strap over the right shoulder and the shield-strap over the left. Monro has both passing over the right shoulder. Leaf points out that Aias evidently wears no breastplate, as ancient critics already noticed. He quotes Herodotus: before the Carians invented shield-handles, warriors steered their shields by leather straps round the neck and left shoulder (1.171). Such a strap suits Aias' huge 'tower' shield of seven ox-hides (7.219-23). The common noun τελαμών, 'strap, support', is also the name of Aias' father Telamon.

title: Hector spun like a top
greek: στρόμβον δ' ὣς ἔσσευε βαλών (strombon d' hōs esseue balōn)
short: Aias hits Hector with one of the stones used to prop the ships and sends him spinning like a child's top.
body: Aias picks up one of the stones that 'rolled amid their feet', the ἔχματα of the ships. LSJ explains these as props or cradles holding the beached hulls upright, and Leaf records Hayman's suggestion of ballast stones. He strikes Hector on the chest above the shield-rim, near the neck, and sets him spinning. στρόμβος is a top (LSJ). Leaf explains it as a whipping-top and notes Virgil's imitation, the maddened Amata whirling like a top whipped by boys (Aen. 7.378-84). He also discusses whether it is Hector or the stone that spins, and the order of events points to Hector. Monro takes it the same way. Comparing the greatest Trojan to a child's toy deflates him sharply.

title: The thunder-struck oak and the smell of sulphur
greek: δεινὴ δὲ θεείου γίγνεται ὀδμή (deinē de theeiou gignetai odmē)
short: Hector falls like an oak uprooted by Zeus's thunderbolt amid a reek of sulphur: a fall that looks like Zeus's work while Zeus is asleep.
body: Hector falls like an oak torn up by the bolt of 'father Zeus', amid a dreadful smell of sulphur that unnerves anyone standing near. Lightning was associated with a sulphurous smell. Zeus's bolt at Diomedes' feet raises a 'terrible flame of burning sulphur' (8.135), and a lightning-struck ship is 'filled with sulphur' (Od. 12.415-17). Leaf (on 16.228) suggests that this association, together with sulphur's volcanic origin, made it seem partly divine. He notes a popular etymology linking θέειον with θεός, 'god', and its use for purification: Akhilleus cleans his cup with it (16.228), and Odysseus fumigates his hall after killing the suitors (Od. 22.481-2). There is irony in the simile, since Zeus is asleep, and Hector, the man his plan favours, falls as though struck by his thunderbolt.

title: Hector carried off and revived at the Xanthus
greek: Ξάνθου δινήεντος, ὃν ἀθάνατος τέκετο Ζεύς (Xanthou dinēentos, hon athanatos teketo Zeus)
short: Hector's comrades carry him to the ford of the Xanthus and revive him with water; he vomits dark blood and falls back unconscious.
body: Polydamas, Aeneas, Agenor, Sarpedon and Glaucus shield the fallen Hector, and his comrades carry him to his chariot. At the ford of the Xanthus they pour water on him. He revives, kneels and vomits dark blood, then sinks back into darkness. Xanthus is the gods' name for the Trojan river Scamander (20.74; Autenrieth), and here he is called the son of Zeus. Leaf notes that ἀθάνατος is very rarely attached to a god's name in Homer. The same line returns at 21.1-2, where Akhilleus reaches the ford, and at 24.692-3, where Priam crosses it bringing Hector's body home. The scene rehearses Hector's death: carried from the field, eyes 'enfolded in black night'. Zeus will later order Apollo to restore him (15.239-62).

title: Satnius and the Naiad: obituaries of minor warriors
greek: ὃν ἄρα νύμφη τέκε νηῒς ἀμύμων (hon ara numphē teke nēïs amumōn)
short: Satnius, son of a river nymph and a herdsman, born by the Satnioeis: a brief birth-story that gives a minor death its weight.
body: Oilean Aias kills Satnius, whom a Naiad nymph bore to Enops as he tended his herds by the river Satnioeis. Leaf explains the name as a short form of 'Satnioeisios', named from the river, like Simoeisios from the Simois (4.474). A Naiad is a water-nymph. Such unions of nymphs and herdsmen recur in the battle-scenes: the Naiad Abarbaree bore twins to Bucolion (6.21-6), and a Naiad bore Iphition (20.382-5). Jasper Griffin showed how these brief biographies of minor warriors, with their birthplaces, parents and herds, lend pathos to deaths that would otherwise be mere names. Naming a man after his native river ties him to a landscape he will not see again.

title: 'See how your Promachus sleeps': the chain of vaunts
greek: φράζεσθ' ὡς ὑμῖν Πρόμαχος δεδμημένος εὕδει (phrazesth' hōs humin Promachos dedmēmenos heudei)
short: Killings and boasts answer each other in turn; Acamas mocks the dead Promachus as 'sleeping' and claims his brother's blood-price.
body: The fighting becomes a sequence of kills and vaunts. Polydamas jeers that his victim will use the spear as a staff on the road to Hades. Monro notes the joke: the dead man needs no other staff. Aias kills Archelochus and asks whether he is not a worthy price for Prothoënor. Acamas then kills Promachus: 'Mark how your Promachus sleeps, vanquished by my spear, so that my brother's blood-price be not long unpaid', which is why a man prays to leave a kinsman at home to avenge him. LSJ cites this line for ποινή as blood-price. 'Sleeps' is the usual euphemism for death (compare 'a sleep of bronze', 11.241), and here it comes while Zeus himself lies asleep on Gargarus. The answering boasts show revenge and honour driving the killing on.

title: Ilioneus' head held up like a poppy
greek: φῆ κώδειαν ἀνασχών (phē kōdeian anaschōn)
short: Peneleos spears Ilioneus through the eye, beheads him, and lifts the head on the spear 'like a poppy-head' to taunt the Trojans.
body: Ilioneus was the only son of Phorbas, rich in flocks, whom Hermes loved. Monro notes that Hermes is here the god of herds. Peneleos drives his spear through Ilioneus' eye, cuts off the head with the helmet still on it, and holds it up with the spear still fixed in the eye, 'like a poppy-head' on its stalk. Leaf follows the ancient reading φή, 'like'. Aristarchus read φῆ, 'he said', and Leaf rejects that construction as unnatural. Peneleos tells the Trojans to bid Ilioneus' parents wail, as Promachus' wife will never welcome her husband home. The image recalls a gentler simile, Gorgythion's head drooping like a poppy heavy with spring rain (8.306-8): there the poppy brings pity, here it is a grisly trophy. The mutilation continues the theme begun with Imbrius' head (13.202-5).

anchor: to bear away the bloody spoils
title: An invocation at the turn of the battle
greek: ἔσπετε νῦν μοι, Μοῦσαι Ὀλύμπια δώματ' ἔχουσαι (espete nun moi, Mousai Olumpia dōmat' echousai)
short: The poet calls on the Muses to name the Greeks who first took spoils once Poseidon turned the battle; a short invocation marking a turning point.
body: 'Tell me now, ye Muses, that have dwellings on Olympus': the poet asks who first took bloody spoils once the Earth-shaker had turned the battle. Then he lists the Greek killers: Telamonian Aias, Antilochus, Meriones, Teucer, Menelaus, and Oilean Aias, fastest in pursuit. The same formula opens the Catalogue of Ships (2.484), and short invocations come at 11.218 and 16.112. Monro reads the appeal and the list as signs that 'we have reached an important turning-point in the story'. Leaf thinks the passage a later addition, since there is no great crisis here, only a temporary ebb of the battle. Elsewhere the Muses are invoked because they are present and know everything, while the poet has only hearsay (2.485-6). At the start of Book 15 Zeus wakes and the tide turns back.
